questions.question: Which of the following best describes the goal of Natural Language Processing (NLP)?

options.text: Enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language
Designing faster CPUs for text rendering
Compiling high-level languages into machine code
Rendering 3D graphics from text descriptions

questions.explanation: NLP is a branch of AI focused on the interaction between computers and human language, including tasks like parsing, understanding, and generating text.

optionsMap.A: Enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language
optionsMap.B: Designing faster CPUs for text rendering
optionsMap.C: Compiling high-level languages into machine code
optionsMap.D: Rendering 3D graphics from text descriptions

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical first step in an NLP pipeline?

options.text: Named Entity Recognition
Tokenization
Sentiment Analysis
Machine Translation

questions.explanation: Tokenization, which splits text into words or subwords, is generally the first step before any further NLP processing.

optionsMap.A: Named Entity Recognition
optionsMap.B: Tokenization
optionsMap.C: Sentiment Analysis
optionsMap.D: Machine Translation

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a typical application of NLP?

options.text: Machine Translation
Sentiment Analysis
Image Segmentation
Named Entity Recognition

questions.explanation: Image segmentation is a computer vision task. NLP applications deal with language tasks like translation, sentiment analysis, and named entity recognition.

optionsMap.A: Machine Translation
optionsMap.B: Sentiment Analysis
optionsMap.C: Image Segmentation
optionsMap.D: Named Entity Recognition

questions.question: In an NLP pipeline, Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging assigns:

options.text: Semantic roles to words
Sentiment scores to sentences
Coreference clusters to pronouns
Grammatical categories (noun, verb, adjective) to each token

questions.explanation: POS tagging labels each token with its grammatical role such as noun, verb, adjective, etc., which is essential for syntactic analysis.

optionsMap.A: Semantic roles to words
optionsMap.B: Sentiment scores to sentences
optionsMap.C: Coreference clusters to pronouns
optionsMap.D: Grammatical categories (noun, verb, adjective) to each token

questions.question: Which NLP task identifies and classifies named entities such as persons, organizations, and locations in text?

options.text: Named Entity Recognition (NER)
Coreference Resolution
Dependency Parsing
Semantic Role Labeling

questions.explanation: NER detects mentions of real-world entities in text and classifies them into predefined categories such as PERSON, ORG, or GPE.

optionsMap.A: Named Entity Recognition (NER)
optionsMap.B: Coreference Resolution
optionsMap.C: Dependency Parsing
optionsMap.D: Semantic Role Labeling

questions.question: What is the fundamental goal of a statistical language model?

options.text: To translate sentences from one language to another
To assign probabilities to sequences of words
To classify images using text labels
To optimize CPU scheduling

questions.explanation: A statistical language model assigns probabilities P(w1, w2, ..., wn) to word sequences, enabling applications like speech recognition and machine translation.

optionsMap.A: To translate sentences from one language to another
optionsMap.B: To assign probabilities to sequences of words
optionsMap.C: To classify images using text labels
optionsMap.D: To optimize CPU scheduling

questions.question: In an n-gram language model, the Markov assumption states that the probability of a word depends on:

options.text: All previous words in the document
Only the next n+1 words
Only the previous n-1 words
A random subset of the vocabulary

questions.explanation: The Markov assumption in n-gram models restricts context to the previous n-1 words, making probability estimation computationally tractable.

optionsMap.A: All previous words in the document
optionsMap.B: Only the next n+1 words
optionsMap.C: Only the previous n-1 words
optionsMap.D: A random subset of the vocabulary

questions.question: What problem does smoothing address in n-gram language models?

options.text: Slow inference speed
Gradient vanishing during training
Overfitting in neural networks
Zero probabilities assigned to unseen n-grams

questions.explanation: When an n-gram was never seen in training, the model assigns zero probability. Smoothing redistributes probability mass to handle these unseen events.

optionsMap.A: Slow inference speed
optionsMap.B: Gradient vanishing during training
optionsMap.C: Overfitting in neural networks
optionsMap.D: Zero probabilities assigned to unseen n-grams

questions.question: Laplace (add-one) smoothing adds a count of 1 to every n-gram. What is the main drawback of this approach?

options.text: It assigns too much probability mass to unseen events
It requires a GPU to compute
It cannot handle bigrams
It only works with neural language models

questions.explanation: Laplace smoothing over-inflates counts for unseen n-grams, taking excessive probability mass away from observed events, especially with large vocabularies.

optionsMap.A: It assigns too much probability mass to unseen events
optionsMap.B: It requires a GPU to compute
optionsMap.C: It cannot handle bigrams
optionsMap.D: It only works with neural language models

questions.question: Kneser-Ney smoothing improves over simpler methods primarily because it uses:

options.text: Word embeddings from pre-trained transformers
Continuation probability based on the number of unique contexts in which a word appears
Beam search to estimate n-gram counts
Gradient descent to learn smoothing parameters

questions.explanation: Kneser-Ney uses continuation probability — the number of distinct contexts a word appears in — which better captures how words generalize to unseen contexts.

optionsMap.A: Word embeddings from pre-trained transformers
optionsMap.B: Continuation probability based on the number of unique contexts in which a word appears
optionsMap.C: Beam search to estimate n-gram counts
optionsMap.D: Gradient descent to learn smoothing parameters

questions.question: Perplexity is commonly used to evaluate language models. A lower perplexity indicates:

options.text: The model is more confused by the test set
The model uses fewer parameters
The model assigns higher probability to the test text, i.e., it is a better model
The model was trained on more data

questions.explanation: Perplexity is the inverse probability of the test set normalized by the number of tokens. Lower perplexity means the model assigns higher probability to actual text.

optionsMap.A: The model is more confused by the test set
optionsMap.B: The model uses fewer parameters
optionsMap.C: The model assigns higher probability to the test text, i.e., it is a better model
optionsMap.D: The model was trained on more data

questions.question: If a language model has perplexity of 100 on a test set, it is roughly equivalent to being as uncertain as:

options.text: Always predicting the correct next word
Using a unigram model
Generating random tokens from a normal distribution
Choosing uniformly at random among 100 words at each step

questions.explanation: Perplexity of k means the model is on average as uncertain as if it were choosing uniformly among k alternatives at each step.

optionsMap.A: Always predicting the correct next word
optionsMap.B: Using a unigram model
optionsMap.C: Generating random tokens from a normal distribution
optionsMap.D: Choosing uniformly at random among 100 words at each step

questions.question: What does the activation function in a neural network primarily enable?

options.text: Non-linear transformations that allow the network to learn complex patterns
Parallelism in GPU computation
Gradient accumulation across mini-batches
Vocabulary lookup in language models

questions.explanation: Without non-linear activation functions, a deep neural network collapses to a single linear transformation. Activations like ReLU allow learning of complex, non-linear functions.

optionsMap.A: Non-linear transformations that allow the network to learn complex patterns
optionsMap.B: Parallelism in GPU computation
optionsMap.C: Gradient accumulation across mini-batches
optionsMap.D: Vocabulary lookup in language models

questions.question: Backpropagation computes gradients using which mathematical rule?

options.text: Product rule only
The chain rule of calculus
L'Hopital's rule
Bayes' theorem

questions.explanation: Backpropagation applies the chain rule of calculus to efficiently compute the gradient of the loss with respect to each parameter in the network.

optionsMap.A: Product rule only
optionsMap.B: The chain rule of calculus
optionsMap.C: L'Hopital's rule
optionsMap.D: Bayes' theorem

questions.question: In a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), the convolution operation is designed to capture:

options.text: Global sequential dependencies across all input positions
Attention weights between all pairs of tokens
Local spatial patterns through shared filter weights
Long-range temporal dependencies in time series

questions.explanation: CNNs use small filters that slide over the input, capturing local patterns efficiently through weight sharing, making them parameter-efficient for spatial data.

optionsMap.A: Global sequential dependencies across all input positions
optionsMap.B: Attention weights between all pairs of tokens
optionsMap.C: Local spatial patterns through shared filter weights
optionsMap.D: Long-range temporal dependencies in time series

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of PyTorch's automatic differentiation (autograd) system?

options.text: It removes the need for GPU hardware
It compiles Python code to C++ for faster execution
It stores all gradients in a relational database
It automatically computes gradients for backpropagation without manual derivation

questions.explanation: PyTorch's autograd builds a dynamic computation graph and automatically computes gradients needed for optimization, freeing researchers from manual gradient derivation.

optionsMap.A: It removes the need for GPU hardware
optionsMap.B: It compiles Python code to C++ for faster execution
optionsMap.C: It stores all gradients in a relational database
optionsMap.D: It automatically computes gradients for backpropagation without manual derivation

questions.question: In PyTorch, what does torch.nn.Module provide?

options.text: A base class for building neural network layers with trainable parameters
A GPU memory allocator
A data loading and preprocessing pipeline
A tokenizer for text input

questions.explanation: torch.nn.Module is the base class for all neural network modules in PyTorch. It manages parameters, enables .forward() overriding, and integrates with the optimizer.

optionsMap.A: A base class for building neural network layers with trainable parameters
optionsMap.B: A GPU memory allocator
optionsMap.C: A data loading and preprocessing pipeline
optionsMap.D: A tokenizer for text input

questions.question: The vanishing gradient problem in deep networks is caused by:

options.text: Gradients becoming too large and causing overflow
Gradients shrinking exponentially as they propagate through many layers with saturating activations
The optimizer using an excessively large learning rate
Dropout randomly removing gradient connections

questions.explanation: With saturating activations like sigmoid or tanh, gradients shrink through each layer of backpropagation, making it difficult to train early layers in deep networks.

optionsMap.A: Gradients becoming too large and causing overflow
optionsMap.B: Gradients shrinking exponentially as they propagate through many layers with saturating activations
optionsMap.C: The optimizer using an excessively large learning rate
optionsMap.D: Dropout randomly removing gradient connections

questions.question: What key limitation do one-hot word representations have that distributed representations (embeddings) overcome?

options.text: One-hot vectors are too small to store
One-hot vectors require GPUs to compute
One-hot vectors treat all words as equally dissimilar, capturing no semantic relationships
One-hot vectors can only represent verbs

questions.explanation: One-hot vectors are orthogonal (zero dot product for any two words), so they encode no semantic similarity. Word embeddings place semantically similar words closer in vector space.

optionsMap.A: One-hot vectors are too small to store
optionsMap.B: One-hot vectors require GPUs to compute
optionsMap.C: One-hot vectors treat all words as equally dissimilar, capturing no semantic relationships
optionsMap.D: One-hot vectors can only represent verbs

questions.question: Word2Vec learns word embeddings by:

options.text: Counting co-occurrence frequencies across all document pairs
Factorizing a TF-IDF matrix using SVD
Clustering documents by topic using LDA
Training a shallow neural network to predict context words (CBOW) or target words from context (Skip-gram)

questions.explanation: Word2Vec uses two architectures: CBOW predicts a word from its context, and Skip-gram predicts context words given a target. Both produce dense word embeddings.

optionsMap.A: Counting co-occurrence frequencies across all document pairs
optionsMap.B: Factorizing a TF-IDF matrix using SVD
optionsMap.C: Clustering documents by topic using LDA
optionsMap.D: Training a shallow neural network to predict context words (CBOW) or target words from context (Skip-gram)

questions.question: Which training technique makes Word2Vec's Skip-gram model computationally efficient by replacing the softmax over the full vocabulary?

options.text: Negative sampling
Hierarchical clustering
L2 regularization
Beam search

questions.explanation: Negative sampling replaces the expensive full softmax with a binary classification task: distinguish the true context word from randomly sampled noise words.

optionsMap.A: Negative sampling
optionsMap.B: Hierarchical clustering
optionsMap.C: L2 regularization
optionsMap.D: Beam search

questions.question: GloVe (Global Vectors for Word Representation) learns embeddings by factorizing:

options.text: A document-term TF-IDF matrix
The log of the global word-word co-occurrence matrix
A neural language model's hidden state matrix
An attention weight matrix from a transformer

questions.explanation: GloVe optimizes an objective that factorizes the log co-occurrence counts of all word pairs, combining statistical advantages of matrix factorization with the efficiency of local context methods.

optionsMap.A: A document-term TF-IDF matrix
optionsMap.B: The log of the global word-word co-occurrence matrix
optionsMap.C: A neural language model's hidden state matrix
optionsMap.D: An attention weight matrix from a transformer

questions.question: How does fastText differ from Word2Vec in representing words?

options.text: fastText uses recurrent neural networks instead of feedforward networks
fastText only works with sentences, not individual words
fastText represents each word as a sum of its character n-gram embeddings, handling morphology and rare words
fastText uses a hierarchical softmax on the output layer only

questions.explanation: fastText extends Word2Vec by breaking words into character n-grams. The word embedding is the sum of its n-gram embeddings, improving performance on rare and morphologically rich words.

optionsMap.A: fastText uses recurrent neural networks instead of feedforward networks
optionsMap.B: fastText only works with sentences, not individual words
optionsMap.C: fastText represents each word as a sum of its character n-gram embeddings, handling morphology and rare words
optionsMap.D: fastText uses a hierarchical softmax on the output layer only

questions.question: Which tokenization strategy is used by GPT-2 and handles rare words by splitting them into frequent subword units?

options.text: Word-level tokenization
Character-level tokenization
SentencePiece with whitespace splitting
Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)

questions.explanation: BPE iteratively merges the most frequent pair of bytes/characters in the corpus, creating a vocabulary of subword units that balances vocabulary size with coverage of rare words.

optionsMap.A: Word-level tokenization
optionsMap.B: Character-level tokenization
optionsMap.C: SentencePiece with whitespace splitting
optionsMap.D: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)

questions.question: WordPiece tokenization (used in BERT) selects merges based on:

options.text: Maximizing the likelihood of the training data when the merge is applied
Maximizing the frequency of the merged pair
Minimizing the perplexity of a bigram model
Alphabetical ordering of candidate merges

questions.explanation: WordPiece selects merges that maximize the language model likelihood of the training data, unlike BPE which just selects the most frequent pair.

optionsMap.A: Maximizing the likelihood of the training data when the merge is applied
optionsMap.B: Maximizing the frequency of the merged pair
optionsMap.C: Minimizing the perplexity of a bigram model
optionsMap.D: Alphabetical ordering of candidate merges

questions.question: Compared to n-gram models, neural language models have the advantage of:

options.text: Being faster to train on small datasets
Generalizing to unseen n-grams through learned continuous representations
Requiring no training data
Using only integer arithmetic

questions.explanation: Neural LMs learn dense embeddings that generalize semantically, so they can assign non-zero probabilities to unseen word sequences based on similar training contexts.

optionsMap.A: Being faster to train on small datasets
optionsMap.B: Generalizing to unseen n-grams through learned continuous representations
optionsMap.C: Requiring no training data
optionsMap.D: Using only integer arithmetic

questions.question: A Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) processes sequential data by:

options.text: Applying a convolution filter in parallel across all positions
Computing self-attention between all pairs of input tokens simultaneously
Maintaining a hidden state that is updated at each time step based on the current input and previous hidden state
Feeding the entire sequence into a feedforward network

questions.explanation: RNNs have a recurrent connection: the hidden state h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t), allowing information from earlier steps to influence later ones.

optionsMap.A: Applying a convolution filter in parallel across all positions
optionsMap.B: Computing self-attention between all pairs of input tokens simultaneously
optionsMap.C: Maintaining a hidden state that is updated at each time step based on the current input and previous hidden state
optionsMap.D: Feeding the entire sequence into a feedforward network

questions.question: The main motivation for Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) over vanilla RNNs is to:

options.text: Enable parallel processing of all sequence positions
Reduce the number of model parameters
Replace the softmax layer with a sigmoid
Mitigate the vanishing gradient problem and capture long-range dependencies

questions.explanation: LSTMs introduce gating mechanisms (input, forget, output gates) and a cell state that allows gradients to flow unchanged over long distances, mitigating vanishing gradients.

optionsMap.A: Enable parallel processing of all sequence positions
optionsMap.B: Reduce the number of model parameters
optionsMap.C: Replace the softmax layer with a sigmoid
optionsMap.D: Mitigate the vanishing gradient problem and capture long-range dependencies

questions.question: How does a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) differ from an LSTM?

options.text: GRU combines the forget and input gates into a single update gate and has no separate cell state
GRU uses three gates: input, output, and forget
GRU has no recurrent connections
GRU is only used in transformer encoders

questions.explanation: GRU simplifies LSTM with two gates (reset and update) and merges the cell state with the hidden state, giving comparable performance with fewer parameters.

optionsMap.A: GRU combines the forget and input gates into a single update gate and has no separate cell state
optionsMap.B: GRU uses three gates: input, output, and forget
optionsMap.C: GRU has no recurrent connections
optionsMap.D: GRU is only used in transformer encoders

questions.question: In a sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) model for machine translation, the encoder's role is to:

options.text: Generate the output sentence word by word
Compress the input sequence into a fixed-length context vector (or set of hidden states)
Compute attention weights over the target sentence
Apply beam search to select the best output

questions.explanation: The encoder processes the source sentence and produces a context representation; the decoder then generates the target sentence conditioned on this context.

optionsMap.A: Generate the output sentence word by word
optionsMap.B: Compress the input sequence into a fixed-length context vector (or set of hidden states)
optionsMap.C: Compute attention weights over the target sentence
optionsMap.D: Apply beam search to select the best output

questions.question: What is the main limitation of greedy decoding in sequence generation?

options.text: It requires exponential memory
It always selects the globally optimal sequence
It may select locally optimal tokens that lead to suboptimal overall sequences
It cannot be parallelized on GPUs

questions.explanation: Greedy decoding picks the highest-probability token at each step, potentially missing sequences that are globally better because early choices foreclose better later options.

optionsMap.A: It requires exponential memory
optionsMap.B: It always selects the globally optimal sequence
optionsMap.C: It may select locally optimal tokens that lead to suboptimal overall sequences
optionsMap.D: It cannot be parallelized on GPUs

questions.question: Beam search with beam width k keeps track of:

options.text: k randomly sampled complete sequences
All possible sequences up to length k
k different temperature values for sampling
The k most probable partial sequences at each decoding step

questions.explanation: Beam search maintains the top-k partial hypotheses at each step, expanding each and keeping the best k, balancing quality and computational cost.

optionsMap.A: k randomly sampled complete sequences
optionsMap.B: All possible sequences up to length k
optionsMap.C: k different temperature values for sampling
optionsMap.D: The k most probable partial sequences at each decoding step

questions.question: In temperature sampling, setting temperature T close to 0 produces:

options.text: Nearly deterministic outputs (similar to greedy decoding)
More diverse and creative outputs
Uniform random token selection
A sequence of rare words

questions.explanation: Temperature T < 1 sharpens the distribution; as T approaches 0 it approaches argmax/greedy decoding. T > 1 flattens the distribution, increasing diversity.

optionsMap.A: Nearly deterministic outputs (similar to greedy decoding)
optionsMap.B: More diverse and creative outputs
optionsMap.C: Uniform random token selection
optionsMap.D: A sequence of rare words

questions.question: Top-k sampling restricts token selection to:

options.text: All tokens whose probability exceeds a threshold p
The k tokens with the highest probabilities at each step
k random tokens from the vocabulary
Tokens that appeared in the training corpus at least k times

questions.explanation: Top-k sampling filters the distribution to the k most probable tokens before resampling, preventing very unlikely tokens from being selected.

optionsMap.A: All tokens whose probability exceeds a threshold p
optionsMap.B: The k tokens with the highest probabilities at each step
optionsMap.C: k random tokens from the vocabulary
optionsMap.D: Tokens that appeared in the training corpus at least k times

questions.question: Nucleus (top-p) sampling selects tokens from the smallest set whose cumulative probability exceeds p. This approach handles:

options.text: The fixed vocabulary size problem in beam search
The dynamic context length in RNNs
Variable distribution sharpness — using more candidates when flat and fewer when peaked
The alignment problem in machine translation

questions.explanation: Unlike top-k which uses a fixed number, top-p adapts the candidate set size to the probability distribution, using many tokens when uniform and few when strongly peaked.

optionsMap.A: The fixed vocabulary size problem in beam search
optionsMap.B: The dynamic context length in RNNs
optionsMap.C: Variable distribution sharpness — using more candidates when flat and fewer when peaked
optionsMap.D: The alignment problem in machine translation

questions.question: The attention mechanism in Seq2Seq models allows the decoder to:

options.text: Replace the encoder entirely
Use beam search with variable width
Compute the cross-entropy loss during training
Dynamically focus on different parts of the encoder's output at each decoding step

questions.explanation: Attention produces a weighted sum of encoder hidden states at each decoder step, allowing the decoder to look back at relevant input positions rather than relying solely on a fixed context vector.

optionsMap.A: Replace the encoder entirely
optionsMap.B: Use beam search with variable width
optionsMap.C: Compute the cross-entropy loss during training
optionsMap.D: Dynamically focus on different parts of the encoder's output at each decoding step

questions.question: The Transformer architecture ('Attention Is All You Need') eliminates recurrence in favor of:

options.text: Self-attention mechanisms that process all positions in parallel
Convolutional layers applied to the sequence
LSTM cells with gating
Greedy search for sequence generation

questions.explanation: The Transformer replaces RNN recurrence with self-attention, enabling full parallelism during training and direct modeling of long-range dependencies.

optionsMap.A: Self-attention mechanisms that process all positions in parallel
optionsMap.B: Convolutional layers applied to the sequence
optionsMap.C: LSTM cells with gating
optionsMap.D: Greedy search for sequence generation

questions.question: In the scaled dot-product attention mechanism, the scaling factor 1/sqrt(dk) is used to:

options.text: Normalize the output to have unit variance
Prevent dot products from growing too large and pushing softmax into regions with tiny gradients
Ensure queries and keys have integer values
Speed up matrix multiplication on GPUs

questions.explanation: For large dk, the dot products grow in magnitude, pushing softmax into regions where gradients nearly vanish. Scaling by 1/sqrt(dk) counteracts this.

optionsMap.A: Normalize the output to have unit variance
optionsMap.B: Prevent dot products from growing too large and pushing softmax into regions with tiny gradients
optionsMap.C: Ensure queries and keys have integer values
optionsMap.D: Speed up matrix multiplication on GPUs

questions.question: Multi-head attention uses multiple attention heads primarily to:

options.text: Reduce the total number of parameters compared to single-head attention
Increase the sequence length the model can process
Allow the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions
Perform position-wise feedforward operations

questions.explanation: Each head learns to attend to different types of relationships (syntactic, semantic, etc.) in parallel, and their outputs are concatenated and projected.

optionsMap.A: Reduce the total number of parameters compared to single-head attention
optionsMap.B: Increase the sequence length the model can process
optionsMap.C: Allow the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions
optionsMap.D: Perform position-wise feedforward operations

questions.question: Why do Transformers need positional encoding?

options.text: To provide labels for supervised training
To initialize the query and key matrices
To reduce the vocabulary size
Because self-attention is permutation-equivariant and has no inherent sense of token order

questions.explanation: Self-attention treats inputs as a set (order-invariant). Positional encodings inject token position information into the embeddings so the model can use sequence order.

optionsMap.A: To provide labels for supervised training
optionsMap.B: To initialize the query and key matrices
optionsMap.C: To reduce the vocabulary size
optionsMap.D: Because self-attention is permutation-equivariant and has no inherent sense of token order

questions.question: Layer Normalization in a Transformer normalizes activations:

options.text: Across the feature dimension for each individual example (token)
Across the batch dimension for each feature
Across the time dimension for each batch element
Only during inference, not training

questions.explanation: Layer Norm normalizes across the feature (embedding) dimension within each token's representation, making it independent of batch size and suitable for sequences of varying length.

optionsMap.A: Across the feature dimension for each individual example (token)
optionsMap.B: Across the batch dimension for each feature
optionsMap.C: Across the time dimension for each batch element
optionsMap.D: Only during inference, not training

questions.question: The original Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) uses which normalization placement?

options.text: Pre-LN: LayerNorm is applied before the sub-layer
Post-LN: LayerNorm is applied after the residual addition
Both Pre-LN and Post-LN in alternate layers
Neither; it uses Batch Normalization

questions.explanation: The original Transformer paper uses Post-LN, applying LayerNorm after the residual connection. Later works (GPT-2, GPT-3) often prefer Pre-LN for more stable training.

optionsMap.A: Pre-LN: LayerNorm is applied before the sub-layer
optionsMap.B: Post-LN: LayerNorm is applied after the residual addition
optionsMap.C: Both Pre-LN and Post-LN in alternate layers
optionsMap.D: Neither; it uses Batch Normalization

questions.question: The time complexity of the self-attention operation with respect to sequence length n is:

options.text: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(n squared)
O(n cubed)

questions.explanation: Computing attention scores requires a pairwise comparison of all n x n token pairs, resulting in O(n^2) time and memory complexity with respect to sequence length.

optionsMap.A: O(n log n)
optionsMap.B: O(n)
optionsMap.C: O(n squared)
optionsMap.D: O(n cubed)

questions.question: ELMo (Embeddings from Language Models) generates context-dependent word representations by:

options.text: Training a GPT-style decoder-only transformer
Computing dot-product attention over all words in the vocabulary
Fine-tuning BERT on a named entity recognition task
Combining hidden states from all layers of a bidirectional LSTM language model

questions.explanation: ELMo computes representations by weighting and combining all layer outputs from a biLSTM trained on language modeling, producing context-sensitive embeddings.

optionsMap.A: Training a GPT-style decoder-only transformer
optionsMap.B: Computing dot-product attention over all words in the vocabulary
optionsMap.C: Fine-tuning BERT on a named entity recognition task
optionsMap.D: Combining hidden states from all layers of a bidirectional LSTM language model

questions.question: BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) is pre-trained using which two objectives?

options.text: Masked Language Modeling (MLM) and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP)
Machine translation and image captioning
Autoregressive language modeling and sentence classification
Named entity recognition and dependency parsing

questions.explanation: BERT is pre-trained with MLM (predicting randomly masked tokens) and NSP (predicting if sentence B follows sentence A), enabling rich bidirectional representations.

optionsMap.A: Masked Language Modeling (MLM) and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP)
optionsMap.B: Machine translation and image captioning
optionsMap.C: Autoregressive language modeling and sentence classification
optionsMap.D: Named entity recognition and dependency parsing

questions.question: In BERT's Masked Language Model (MLM), what percentage of tokens are randomly masked during pre-training?
questions.explanation: BERT randomly masks 15% of tokens. Of those, 80% are replaced with [MASK], 10% with a random token, and 10% left unchanged, to reduce the mismatch between pre-training and fine-tuning.

questions.question: Encoder-only models like BERT are best suited for which type of tasks?

options.text: Open-ended text generation
Code completion and code generation
Language understanding tasks such as classification, NER, and question answering
Summarization and translation

questions.explanation: Encoder-only models have full bidirectional attention and are ideal for understanding tasks. They are not designed for auto-regressive generation.

optionsMap.A: Open-ended text generation
optionsMap.B: Code completion and code generation
optionsMap.C: Language understanding tasks such as classification, NER, and question answering
optionsMap.D: Summarization and translation

questions.question: GPT-style decoder-only models use which type of attention mask during pre-training?
